Illustration only Photo by Tim Doerfler on Unsplash GM’s Patent May One Day Decide Who Drives? In Wisconsin, driver’s licenses are renewed based on eyesight, not age. But new technology from GM may upend that balance. A recently filed patent would allow cars themselves to decide whether you’re safe to drive — a move that has seniors and advocacy groups worried about losing independence. MSN . The idea is provocative: should automakers, not the DMV, be the ones to take aging drivers off the road?
That question hits home in Wisconsin, where the state has no legal maximum driving age. Instead, the privilege to drive rests entirely on a person’s ability to meet health and vision standards.
Wisconsin’s Rules for Senior Drivers Unlike some states that impose special retesting once drivers hit 70 or 75, Wisconsin law is straightforward:
No Age Limit : A 90-year-old and a 30-year-old are held to the same renewal rules. License Renewal : Every 8 years, drivers must renew their licenses with the Wisconsin DMV ( WisDOT ). Vision Requirements : At least 20/40 vision in each eye (with or without corrective lenses) and a 70° horizontal field of vision from the center. Minimum for restricted licensing is 20/100 in one eye and 20° field of vision . Possible Restrictions : If vision doesn’t fully meet the standard, WisDOT may impose limits such as: Daylight-only driving Mandatory use of corrective lenses Outside rear-view mirror requirement Restricted routes or areas If a driver’s eyesight falls below even the restricted standards, they may be referred for a medical review or road test.
The Balancing Act: Freedom vs. Safety For many seniors, driving isn’t just mobility—it’s independence. Removing that privilege can be devastating. Wisconsin’s system avoids blanket age limits and instead focuses on whether a person can safely operate a vehicle in real conditions.
But with GM’s patent hinting at a future where cars themselves monitor ability, the debate may soon shift. Could AI-enabled cars end up deciding when someone’s too old—or too impaired—to drive?
Bottom Line for Wisconsin Drivers Wisconsin has no age ceiling for drivers. Vision standards are the gatekeeper for license renewals. Conditions like glaucoma, cataracts, or other progressive eye diseases can trigger extra reviews. Tech like GM’s patent may change the conversation, but for now, it’s your eyesight—not your birthdate—that determines your right to drive in Wisconsin. Enjoy this story? Stay connected:
